section.title: Bitter Providence in Moab
section.sectionRationale: The book opens with a compressed tragedy that sets up everything to follow. In the lawless days of the judges, famine drives an Israelite family from Bethlehem to Moab, and within five verses a husband and two sons are dead and Naomi is left empty. It is one tight scene of loss that raises the question the rest of the book answers: is God present in this darkness?
section.thesis: In a time of spiritual chaos, a family flees the house of bread for a foreign land, and death empties Naomi of everything; yet the very sorrows that look like abandonment are the opening moves of a hidden and faithful providence.
section.frameNote: One dark scene in three beats: the flight from Bethlehem to Moab; the death of Elimelech; and the death of both sons, leaving Naomi bereft.

units.label: Famine drives a family to Moab

verses.text: In the days when the judges ruled, there was a {{famine|famine}} in the land. And a certain man from {{bethlehem|Bethlehem}} in Judah, with his wife and two sons, went to reside in the land of Moab.

The man’s name was Elimelech, his wife’s name was {{naomi|Naomi}}, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah, and they entered the land of Moab and settled there.
Then Naomi’s husband Elimelech died, and she was left with her two sons,
who took Moabite women as their wives, one named Orpah and the other named Ruth. And after they had lived in Moab about ten years,
both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and Naomi was left without her two sons and without her husband.

famine.gloss: Famine, hunger, a failure of food. In the covenant, famine could signal God's discipline on a wayward people, Deuteronomy 28. Here it drives an Israelite family out of the promised land in search of bread, setting the whole story in motion.

bethlehem.gloss: House of bread. The name carries a sharp irony: a famine empties the house of bread, so the family leaves it for Moab. In time the true bread will come from Bethlehem, first the line of David, and at last Jesus, the bread of life, Micah 5:2 and John 6:35.

naomi.gloss: Pleasant, lovely, sweet. Her name frames the tragedy of the book: the pleasant one is stripped of husband and sons and will soon ask to be called Mara, bitter. The movement from full to empty and back again drives the whole of chapter one.

basic.context: The book of Ruth is set in the days of the judges, a dark and lawless time when everyone did as they saw fit. A famine hits Bethlehem, and a man named Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to live in Moab, a foreign and often hostile land. There the father dies, the sons marry Moabite women, and then both sons die too, leaving Naomi with nothing.
basic.hermeneutics: This is history told with great economy: five verses cover ten years and three deaths. The narrator does not scold Elimelech directly, so readers debate whether leaving Bethlehem was faithless or simply desperate. Either way, the point is the depth of Naomi's loss and the quiet truth that God has not disappeared, even when life looks like pure disaster.
basic.originalLanguages: The famine, ra'ab, empties Bethlehem, whose name means house of bread. Naomi's name means pleasant, which makes her coming grief all the sharper. These names are not decoration; they set up the reversals the whole book will trace.
basic.typology: Naomi's emptying, a journey out of the land into exile and loss, echoes Israel's own story and points ahead to the pattern of death before resurrection. The empty womb and empty home will be filled by a redeemer, a shadow of the greater emptying and filling accomplished in Christ.
basic.christ: Bethlehem, the house of bread, is where this sorrow begins, and it is where the Saviour will one day be born. The famine and death that empty Naomi begin a story that runs straight to David and on to Jesus, showing that God was weaving redemption even through the family's darkest days.
basic.god: Though God is never named as acting in these verses, He is the unseen author of the whole account. We learn that God's providence is often hidden inside suffering, that He does not abandon His people in their grief, and that He can begin a work of rescue in what looks like the end of everything.
basic.crossReferences: Judges 21 sets the lawless backdrop. Genesis 12 and 26 show earlier famines that tested faith. Micah 5 promises a ruler from Bethlehem, and Matthew 1 will place Ruth in that very line.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's big story of a God who redeems the lost begins here in miniature: an empty, grieving woman in a foreign land. From this bitter start God will bring a kinsman-redeemer, a royal line, and finally the Christ, proving that no darkness is beyond the reach of His quiet, faithful purpose.

context.literary: These five verses are pure narration, without a single word of direct speech, a deliberate contrast with the chapter's second half, verses 6 through 22, which is almost entirely dialogue. The effect is a rapid, almost breathless overture: a chain of bare verbs, went, entered, settled, died, took, lived, died, carries ten years and three deaths in the space most narratives would spend on a single scene. The book's opening formula, in the days when the judges ruled, deliberately echoes the recurring introductions that begin each cycle in the book of Judges, though it swaps that book's usual moral indictment, the Israelites did evil, for a bare circumstance, there was a famine, inviting the reader to wonder from the very first line whether the two kinds of trouble, sin and hardship, are as separable in this era as the narrator's restraint suggests. The unit moves geographically outward, Bethlehem to Moab, and its structure of departure will be answered, almost verse for verse, by the return that fills the rest of the chapter; readers are meant to feel the outward pull here so that the pull homeward in verses 6 and following lands with its full weight. Even the order of the deaths matters: husband first, then, after a decade's gap marked only by a subordinate clause about marriage, both sons together, so that Naomi's loss escalates rather than arriving all at once.
context.historical: Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, a plateau close enough to Bethlehem that a family in real distress could reach it within days, which likely explains why Elimelech's household, rather than some more distant country, becomes the destination. The nation traced its origin to Lot's older daughter, Genesis 19:37, a shameful beginning by Israel's own account, and its relations with Israel across the centuries were rarely peaceful: Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel from Moab's plains, Numbers 22 through 24, Moabite women drew Israelite men into the worship of Baal of Peor, Numbers 25, and a Moabite king, Eglon, later oppressed Israel for eighteen years before Ehud's deliverance, Judges 3:12-30. Moab's own god, Chemosh, is named often enough elsewhere in the Old Testament to make its presence in this family's new home unavoidable; a household seeking food would also be a household living daily among Chemosh's worshipers. Famine itself was an ordinary hazard of an agrarian society without irrigation on the scale of Egypt or Mesopotamia, dependent entirely on seasonal rain, so a single failed harvest in Judah could mean genuine hunger while a neighboring, better watered region still had grain, exactly the asymmetry that later sends Naomi home again once word comes that the LORD has provided bread in Judah. The days when the judges ruled were themselves marked by cycles of apostasy, oppression, and deliverance recorded throughout the book of Judges, a chaotic backdrop against which one ordinary family's private disaster unfolds without any judge, any deliverer, and for these five verses, any mention of the LORD acting at all.
context.canonical: Ruth stands between Judges and Samuel in the English canon, and its opening line reads almost like a deliberate hinge, borrowing the era from the book before it while refusing to borrow that book's verdict of moral collapse. Where Judges ends, there was no king in Israel, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Judges 21:25, Ruth opens onto a private household making an understandable, perhaps unwise, decision under pressure, the same era, a very different texture. Genesis had already established the pattern of famine sending a patriarch's family out of the land, Abram to Egypt, Genesis 12:10, Isaac nearly following him there before God stops him, Genesis 26:1-2, so Elimelech's move fits an old and recurring test of faith rather than introducing something new. What the earlier famines never did was end in three deaths, with a foreign land turning out, unexpectedly, to hold the family's future rather than merely its temporary survival. The book's last verses will trace this family's line through Boaz and Obed to Jesse and David, 4:18-22, so that the New Testament can list Ruth by name in the genealogy that opens the Gospel of Matthew, 1:5. Nothing in these first five verses hints at that outcome; it is the canonical shape of the whole Bible that lets a reader see, retrospectively, that a decade of famine, foreign residence, and grief was never outside the story God was already writing toward Bethlehem's second, greater birth.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The narrator compresses ten years and three deaths into five verses precisely so that the reader arrives at verse 6 with Naomi, not lingering over the causes of Elimelech's decision but sitting inside the weight of what it cost. Nothing in the account signals blame, no charge of sin, no divine rebuke, which is itself an authorial choice: had the writer wanted a morality tale about the danger of leaving the land, he had ready-made vocabulary for it elsewhere in the Torah and used none of it here. Instead he wants readers to feel the ordinariness of the disaster, a family does what many prudent families would do in famine, and disaster still finds them, so that whatever hope the rest of the book offers cannot be read as a reward for having made a better decision than Elimelech. The author's aim in this opening unit is to establish loss as flat, historical fact before introducing, in the very next verse, the first hint that this same flat history is secretly the LORD's own story.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: These verses record a sequence of events; they legislate nothing. The famine, the move, the marriages, and the deaths are reported as what happened to this family, not as a pattern later households are commanded to follow or avoid. Readers should resist turning Elimelech's move into a fixed rule, either that leaving hardship for a foreign land is always faithless or that it is always wise; the text's own restraint refuses to settle that question for us, which is part of the point. What the passage does teach, without needing to command it, is realistic: famine, displacement, and death belong to life under the fall, and Scripture will not pretend otherwise to make a tidier moral. The enduring application is not a rule about geography but a posture, honest acknowledgment of loss, held open to whatever God may yet be doing within it.

debates.question: Was Elimelech's move to Moab a sinful failure of faith or an understandable act of survival?

views.label: A faithless departure
views.case: He left the promised land and the house of bread for a pagan enemy nation, and his sons then married Moabite women; the string of deaths that follows is often read as the sad fruit of leaving the place of covenant blessing.

views.label: An understandable flight from famine
views.case: The text never openly condemns him; the patriarchs too moved during famine, and the narrator's restraint suggests the focus is on Naomi's suffering and God's providence, not on assigning blame.

debates.bearing: Either reading leaves the main point intact: real loss unfolds in a broken world, and God is quietly at work to redeem it, whatever the mix of human fault and circumstance.

debates.question: Did Mahlon and Chilion sin by marrying Moabite women?

views.label: A clear violation
views.case: Deuteronomy 7:3-4 forbids intermarriage that would turn Israel's heart after other gods, and Moab's national god Chemosh made such unions especially dangerous; the string of deaths that follows reads to some as the fruit of a doubly compromised household.

views.label: Not directly forbidden
views.case: The explicit ban in Deuteronomy 7 names the Canaanite nations, not Moab, and Deuteronomy 23:3 excludes Moabites from Israel's assembly without addressing marriage directly; the narrator records the marriages, verse 4, without a word of rebuke, which many take as evidence the text is not building a case against intermarriage as such.

debates.bearing: Either way the story does not ask readers to imitate Elimelech's household as a model; it asks them to watch what God does next with a Moabite daughter-in-law who will prove more loyal to Israel's God than many Israelites, turning a doubtful marriage into the doorway of grace.

study.originalLanguages:
Ra'ab, famine, is covenant vocabulary before it is meteorology. Deuteronomy 28:23-24 warns that a bronze sky and iron ground, no rain, no harvest, would follow a broken covenant, so that any hearer trained in Torah could not read of famine striking the land without wondering whether some deeper unfaithfulness lay behind it, even though the text itself never says so here. The narrator's silence on cause is itself notable restraint; he reports the famine the way he reports the coming deaths, without commentary.

The verb that describes the family's move is gwr, to sojourn, the technical term for living as a resident alien with no inherited land and no full civic standing, the very word used of Abraham in Canaan and of Israel in Egypt. Yet by verse 2 the text has shifted to yashab, to settle or dwell, entered the land of Moab and settled there, and by verse 4 ten years have passed. What began as a temporary sojourn to outlast a famine becomes, almost without the narrator remarking on it, a permanent settlement in a land Israel had long been warned against, Deuteronomy 23:3-6. The grammar tracks a drift the family itself may never have consciously chosen.

Beth lechem, house of bread, is the very place the family leaves because it cannot supply what its name promises, and the family goes instead to Moab, a land whose produce, by the time of Ruth's return, will turn out to be barley and grain enough to feed two widows, a reversal chapter two makes plain.

Elimelech's own name, eli, my God, and melek, king, together mean my God is king, a confession spoken by a man whose era, per Judges 21:25, has no king in Israel at all, and who now dies far from the land where that God's kingship was meant to be lived out. The irony sits quietly in the text, unremarked, the way this whole scene refuses to moralize even as it reports one loss after another.

Naomi, pleasant, closes the unit as it opened, a woman named for sweetness who will soon rename herself, though that renaming belongs to the verses just ahead, sits at the center of a household about to be stripped of everything the name once described.

typology.type: Naomi's exile and emptying in a foreign land
typology.fulfillment: Naomi leaves the promised land for Moab still full, a husband and two sons beside her, and will return having lost all three, an emptying so complete she will ask to be renamed for it. Scripture regularly uses exile and loss as the dark side of a pattern that ends in return and restoration, most fully in the pattern of death before resurrection, in which Christ is emptied to the point of the grave before He is raised and exalted, Philippians 2:6-11. Naomi's story does not reach resurrection in these five verses, only loss, but the book will not leave her there, and neither does the larger pattern her emptying belongs to.

typology.type: Bethlehem, the house of bread struck by famine
typology.fulfillment: A famine empties Bethlehem, the house of bread, of the very thing its name promises, forcing a family to seek food outside the land God had given them. The irony is corrected centuries later when this same town becomes the birthplace of Jesus, who names Himself the bread of life and promises that whoever comes to Him will never hunger, John 6:35, and whom Micah foretells will come from Bethlehem Ephrathah to be ruler over Israel, Micah 5:2. The house of bread that could not feed its own family in chapter one becomes, in the end, the source of bread for the whole world.

typology.type: A Bethlehem family that flees danger to a foreign land and later returns
typology.fulfillment: Elimelech takes his household out of Bethlehem to escape a famine, sojourning in Moab until word comes that it is safe to return. Centuries later another Bethlehem family flees a different danger, Herod's massacre of the children, taking the infant Jesus down to Egypt until it is safe to return, Matthew 2:13-15, a flight the Gospel of Matthew ties to Hosea's word, out of Egypt I called My Son, Hosea 11:1. Both departures are for survival, not unbelief, and both endings bring the family back toward the land of promise. Elimelech's return is broken and grieving, but the return from Egypt carries the Savior who will finally undo every grief a fallen world can inflict.

study.christ:
Elimelech's own name confesses more than he can yet see fulfilled, my God is king. He dies in Moab in an era with no king in Israel at all, Judges 21:25, a bitter irony that only resolves generations later when a true King is born in the very town Elimelech left, a King whose kingdom this whole family's grief was quietly serving even in its worst hour.

The pattern of a Bethlehem household fleeing danger to a foreign land finds an exact echo in Matthew's account of the infant Jesus. Herod's massacre of the children sends Joseph and Mary to Egypt for safety, and Matthew reads their return as a fulfillment of Hosea's word, out of Egypt I called My Son, Matthew 2:13-15 and Hosea 11:1. Elimelech's flight is for bread, not from a murderous king, and his family's flight ends in death rather than deliverance, but both stories begin in the same town and both trace a movement outward before a movement back, so that when the greater Son of Bethlehem returns from Egypt unharmed, the earlier, sadder departure reads almost like a shadow the true story finally answers in full.

There is a second, quieter thread. Two of Elimelech's household will marry Moabite women, verse 4, and though neither the narrator nor Naomi yet knows it, one of those marriages is already carrying the ancestry of the Messiah forward, since Ruth will become the great-grandmother of David and stand in the genealogy that opens Matthew's Gospel. The line that runs to Christ is, from its earliest visible moment in this book, already running through a foreign woman's marriage into an Israelite family, long before anyone in the story can see what God is doing with it.

Above all, this opening scene establishes exactly the kind of hopeless material the gospel specializes in redeeming. A dead husband, two dead sons, a childless decade, none of it looks like the beginning of anything good, and that is the point: the Christ who will be born in this same Bethlehem specializes in turning graves into the starting line of resurrection, and this family's grief, though the text does not yet say so, is already inside that larger story.
study.god:
Not one verb in this unit is attributed to the LORD, yet the whole unit assumes His rule over exactly the kinds of things it records, harvests and their failure, life and its end. Deuteronomy's own theology insists that the LORD, not any Canaanite or Moabite deity, holds these powers, I bring death and I give life, Deuteronomy 32:39, so an Israelite reader could not read of famine in the land and death in a foreign field without assuming, even in the narrator's silence, that these events unfold under a sovereignty wider than either Israel's or Moab's borders. The family sojourns in a land whose god, Chemosh, claimed authority over exactly this kind of fertility and mortality; the narrator's refusal to credit Chemosh with anything, indeed to credit any god by name with these events until Naomi speaks in the verses just ahead, is itself a theological statement. Nothing happens outside the reach of Israel's God, not even in Moab, not even to a family that has, in effect, left His land.

This raises, without resolving, the oldest problem believers face: why the faithful and the merely ordinary alike suffer famine, exile, and death together, seemingly without discrimination. The text offers no easy answer here; it simply reports the losses and waits. That restraint is itself a kind of honesty about God's ways that Scripture elsewhere makes explicit, how unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways, Romans 11:33, a truth Naomi will state in her own blunter words a few verses later. What this opening unit teaches about God, before anyone in the story says a word about Him, is that His governance does not depend on being named to be real, and that the same sovereignty that permits a famine and three deaths in five verses is patient enough to let a whole book unfold before showing its purpose. Readers who want God's presence proven by a miracle in every verse will find this unit disappointing; readers willing to trust a hidden hand will find, by the book's end, that the hand was never absent, only unannounced.

crossReferences.note: The verse that closes the book just before Ruth begins: there was no king in Israel, everyone did what was right in his own eyes. Ruth 1:1 opens in that same lawless period, yet tells a story of ordinary hardship rather than atrocity, showing that even a chaotic era held quieter, private griefs alongside its public ones.

Abram takes his household to Egypt when famine strikes Canaan, the first instance of a patriarch leaving the promised land under the pressure of hunger. Elimelech's move to Moab follows the same well worn path, and Genesis never condemns Abram outright for it either, though that visit brings its own trouble, Genesis 12:14-20.

When a famine strikes in Isaac's day, the LORD specifically tells him not to go down to Egypt but to stay in the land He names. No such word reaches Elimelech; the narrator's silence about any divine instruction, for or against leaving, is conspicuous next to this earlier episode where God does speak.

Moab is named for the son born to Lot's older daughter after Sodom's destruction, a shameful origin by Israel's own telling. That a family from Bethlehem settles among this nation, and that its women will later marry into Israel, sets up the surprising grace the rest of the book of Ruth will trace.

Among the curses for covenant unfaithfulness, the LORD warns of a bronze sky and iron ground, no rain and no harvest. The narrator never says Judah's famine in Ruth 1:1 is such a judgment, but any reader trained in this warning would hear it echoing behind the bare word famine.

Bethlehem Ephrathah, small among the clans of Judah, will bring forth the one to be ruler over Israel. The very town famine empties in these opening verses is named centuries in advance as the birthplace of that ruler, a promise this family could not have known while grieving inside it.

The genealogy that opens the New Testament lists Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, and David, tracing a line that this chapter's tragedy will, unknown to anyone in it, eventually feed. Two of the very deaths recorded in Ruth 1:3-5 stand upstream of a family tree that ends at Jesus, called Christ, Matthew 1:16.

Another Bethlehem family flees to a foreign land under threat, Herod's massacre of the children, and later returns, an episode Matthew reads as a fulfillment of Hosea's word, out of Egypt I called My Son. The pattern of departure and return that opens the book of Ruth echoes forward into the Messiah's own infancy.

Isaiah promises a feast of rich food for every people on God's mountain, and that the LORD will swallow up death forever, wiping every tear away. Both griefs of Ruth 1:1-5, hunger and death, are named here as things God Himself will finally undo, not merely relieve for one family in one generation.

The Bible's last vision answers this opening one directly: no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away. The famine and the three graves that open the book of Ruth belong to a world Revelation promises will not have the last word.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 3 introduced two griefs this short unit lives inside: the ground would resist human labor and yield thorns rather than freely giving bread, Genesis 3:17-19, and death, once a threat, would become an appointment every family eventually keeps. Bethlehem's famine and then Elimelech's, Mahlon's, and Chilion's deaths are the fall working itself out in one ordinary household centuries later, a small case study in the larger pattern every reader of Genesis 3 already expects, that a world east of Eden supplies neither guaranteed bread nor guaranteed years.

Yet the fall is never the last word Scripture allows itself. Isaiah pictures a coming feast of rich food for all peoples on God's mountain, where He will swallow up death forever and wipe away every tear, Isaiah 25:6-8, promises that answer, point for point, the two griefs this unit records, hunger and death. Revelation closes the whole Bible with the same two promises fulfilled without remainder, no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and a tree bearing fruit for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2.

Between the fall in Genesis and that final feast stands this ordinary tragedy, easy to skip past on the way to Ruth's more famous scenes, and yet exactly the kind of raw material redemption specializes in. Nothing here has been fixed yet; a widow stands in a foreign field with nothing recovered and no rescuer named. But the whole shape of the Bible's story, creation good, fall broken, redemption promised, new creation certain, is what allows a reader who knows how the story ends to read Naomi's opening disaster as a tragedy still working itself toward an ending the family in this chapter cannot yet imagine. The famine that empties Bethlehem here will be answered, within a single chapter, by a harvest, and the deaths that empty Naomi will be answered, by the book's last verse, with a grandson placed in her arms.

sermon.title: “Can This Be Naomi?”
sermon.why: The opening message of Begg's expository series A Study in Ruth, working from Ruth 1:1 through the family's flight to Moab and the deaths that empty Naomi, showing God's providence at work in the ordinary and the tragic. A clear, orthodox handling of this movement's setting and losses.

quiz.q: What time period is the book of Ruth set in?

options.text: The days when the judges ruled, a lawless and unsettled era in Israel.
options.note: Ruth 1:1 places the story in the turbulent days of the judges.

options.text: The reign of King David.
options.note: David is the goal the book points to, but the events happen before his reign, in the judges era.

options.text: The years of Israel's exile in Babylon.
options.note: That exile is centuries later; Ruth is set in the judges period.

options.text: The time of Moses and the wilderness wandering.
options.note: That is much earlier; Ruth belongs to the settled but chaotic judges era.

quiz.q: Why did Elimelech take his family to Moab?

options.text: A famine had struck the land, and he sought food and survival abroad.
options.note: Ruth 1:1 names the famine as the reason for the move.

options.text: God commanded him to settle in Moab.
options.note: There is no such command; the move was driven by famine, not a divine call.

options.text: He was fleeing a war in Bethlehem.
options.note: The text names famine, not war, as the cause.

options.text: He wanted to marry his sons to Moabite women.
options.note: The marriages came later; the move itself was for food during the famine.

quiz.q: What is significant about the name Bethlehem in this opening?

options.text: It means house of bread, so a famine there is a bitter irony that drives the family away.
options.note: The house of bread is emptied by famine, and later filled by the bread of life.

options.text: It means city of David and honors the coming king.
options.note: Bethlehem does become David's town, but the name means house of bread, which is the irony here.

options.text: It was the capital of Moab.
options.note: Bethlehem is in Judah, not Moab; Moab is where they flee to.

options.text: It has no meaning worth noting.
options.note: The name is loaded with meaning that the narrator uses on purpose.

quiz.q: By the end of these verses, what has happened to Naomi?

options.text: She has lost her husband and both sons and is left empty in a foreign land.
options.note: Ruth 1:5 states she was left without her two sons and without her husband.

options.text: She has become wealthy in Moab.
options.note: The opposite is true; she is emptied of family, not filled with wealth.

options.text: She has returned safely to Bethlehem.
options.note: That return comes in the next movement; here she is still in Moab and bereaved.

options.text: She has remarried a Moabite man.
options.note: There is no remarriage; she is left a grieving widow.

quiz.q: Where is God in these five verses of loss?

options.text: He is unnamed but not absent; His providence is quietly at work beneath the suffering.
options.note: The hidden hand of God is a central theme of Ruth from the very start.

options.text: He has abandoned the family because of their sin.
options.note: The family suffers, but the book will show God has not abandoned them at all.

options.text: He is actively speaking and commanding throughout the scene.
options.note: God is strikingly silent here; His work is hidden, not spoken.

options.text: He is powerless to help in such a dark time.
options.note: The book reveals God as sovereign over every event, not powerless.

questions: The story opens in a lawless, famine-struck time, yet God is quietly at work. Where in your own hard season might God be present in ways you cannot yet see?
Elimelech left the house of bread for Moab when the pressure came. When trouble hits, are you tempted to run from the place of faith and provision rather than trust God within it?
Naomi lost her husband and both sons in quick succession. How do you hold on to God's goodness when loss piles on loss?
The narrator does not rush to explain or justify the suffering. How does it help to know the Bible tells the truth about grief without tidy answers?
This bitter beginning is the start of a redemption story that leads to Christ. How does knowing the ending change the way you read your own painful chapters?

translationNotes.note: Bethlehem means house of bread, a pointed irony since a famine there is what drives the family out; the same town will later be David's home and the birthplace of Christ.
Ephrathites refers to the clan associated with the region of Bethlehem, also called Ephrathah, tying this family to the promise of Micah 5:2.
The Hebrew stresses that Naomi was left, an emptying that sets up her lament in verses 20 and 21 and the whole book's reversal from empty to full.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Ruth 1:1-5. The clause order in verse 4 follows the BSB, which places the note about ten years in Moab within that verse.
